title: Context, Application, manifest & resources
scopeHtml: Scope: Context types and correct usage, Application class and init order, manifest merging/exported/queries, resource qualifiers/locale/night mode, and app bundle delivery at a high level.

notes.title: Context types
notes.html:
The idea. A Context is your app's handle to the Android system: a pass that lets you open files, start screens, read resources and talk to system services. There are several kinds of pass, and they differ in what they can do and how long they live.

Mechanism. Context is an abstract class. The real work is done by ContextImpl; ContextWrapper forwards every call to a base context; Application, Service and Activity (via ContextThemeWrapper) extend ContextWrapper.

Context (abstract)
  `-- ContextWrapper (holds mBase = ContextImpl)
        |-- Application      lives as long as the process
        |-- Service          lives as long as the service
        `-- ContextThemeWrapper
              `-- Activity   lives as long as the screen (theme + window aware)
Context Can inflate themed views Can start Activity Can show dialog Lifetime
Application no theme (default theme) only with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK no (needs a window token) process
Activity yes yes yes screen
Service no theme needs NEW_TASK no service
ContentProvider/Receiver context limited limited no short

Also: createConfigurationContext, createDisplayContext, createWindowContext (API 30) and createAttributionContext (API 30) return derived contexts with different configuration, display, window type or attribution. A ViewModel should never hold an Activity context; AndroidViewModel hands you the Application.

Industry examples. Room's Room.databaseBuilder(applicationContext, ...), Retrofit/OkHttp caches, Coil/Glide (they take the application context to avoid leaks), WorkManager (WorkManager.getInstance(context) reads context.applicationContext).

Analogy. A building pass: a visitor badge (Application) opens the lobby but not your office; your employee badge (Activity) opens the office, the cafeteria and the meeting room.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the Application context to inflate views or show a dialog: you get wrong theme (a BadTokenException for dialogs).
  • Starting an Activity from a non-Activity context without FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK (AndroidRuntimeException).
  • Believing getApplicationContext() and this are interchangeable for UI work.

notes.title: Which Context to use where
notes.html:
The idea. Choose the context with the shortest life that still does the job, and never store a short-lived one in something long-lived.

Rules of thumb.

  • UI work (views, dialogs, Snackbar, theme attributes, Toast on old versions): Activity context.
  • Anything that outlives a screen (singletons, repositories, DBs, caches, SDK init, WorkManager): Application context.
  • getSystemService works with either; LayoutInflater from an Application context ignores your theme, producing wrong colours.
  • Toast with an Application context works (the window token isn't needed) but custom views lose the theme. Android 11+ restricts background custom toasts.
  • Dialogs, PopupWindow, WindowManager.addView for app windows: Activity context only.
  • In Compose use LocalContext.current, which is the Activity (or a ContextWrapper around it); unwrap with a loop while (ctx is ContextWrapper) { if (ctx is Activity) return ctx; ctx = ctx.baseContext }.
  • Dependency injection: Hilt gives @ApplicationContext and @ActivityContext qualifiers.

Industry examples. Glide with(activity) ties the request to the Activity lifecycle, while with(applicationContext) does not; Picasso and Coil store the application context.

Analogy. Use a hotel room key card only for your room, and the guest-services number (Application) for tasks that continue after you check out.

Common interview traps.

  • Passing the Activity into a singleton "just for convenience".
  • Assuming Application context has the same resource configuration as the Activity (night mode, locale and font scale may differ).
  • Casting a context to Activity without unwrapping ContextWrapper.

notes.title: ContextWrapper and attachBaseContext
notes.html:
The idea. A ContextWrapper is a context that wears another context as a costume and passes calls through. You can swap the costume in order to change behaviour, for example the language.

Mechanism. ContextWrapper.attachBaseContext(Context base) sets mBase. The framework calls it once before onCreate. Override it in an Activity (or Application) to wrap the base with a modified configuration:

override fun attachBaseContext(newBase: Context) {
    val config = Configuration(newBase.resources.configuration)
    config.setLocale(Locale("hi"))
    super.attachBaseContext(newBase.createConfigurationContext(config))
}

Uses: locale override, font scale, custom theme or night mode, multi-dex install (MultiDex.install(base) on API below 21 in Application.attachBaseContext), instrumentation, Dagger/Hilt injection wrappers, ViewPump/Calligraphy (font injection), Kotlin ContextThemeWrapper(base, R.style.Theme) for local theming. Remember attachBaseContext runs before the Application's fields are initialised; do not touch getApplicationContext() there (it returns null).

Industry examples. Libraries like Lingver and ViewPump rely on it; Hilt's generated Hilt_MyActivity hooks injection into onCreate but a wrapper-based DI like Dagger in attachBaseContext was the older approach (ContentProvider-free).

Analogy. A translator who stands between you and a foreign shop owner and rephrases everything you say.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling getApplicationContext() or getResources() before super.attachBaseContext.
  • Wrapping only the Activity context and forgetting that the Application context still has the old locale.
  • Overriding applyOverrideConfiguration incorrectly with AppCompat 1.2+ (locale gets ignored).

notes.title: The Application class and process lifecycle
notes.html:
The idea. One Application object is created per process, before any Activity, Service or Receiver. It is the first place your code runs and the place where global setup belongs, but everything you do there delays startup.

Mechanism. Order for a cold start: Zygote forks, ActivityThread.main, handleBindApplication creates the Application via the manifest android:name, calls attachBaseContext, then installs ContentProviders (installContentProviders, their onCreate), then Application.onCreate, then the first component (Activity onCreate). Hence ContentProviders run before Application.onCreate. Application stays alive until the process dies; there is no reliable onTerminate on real devices (only in emulators). onTrimMemory(level) and onLowMemory are callbacks for pressure; registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks and ProcessLifecycleOwner (androidx.lifecycle) track foreground/background; ActivityLifecycleCallbacks suits analytics.

Multi-process caution. Components declared with android:process=":remote" get their own process and their own Application instance, so Application.onCreate runs again and initialises everything twice (Firebase, Crashlytics, DI, WorkManager) and wastes memory. Guard with Application.getProcessName() (API 28) or ActivityManager.runningAppProcesses, or a isMainProcess helper.

Industry examples. Firebase initialises through a ContentProvider (FirebaseInitProvider); Timber/Crashlytics/Hilt (@HiltAndroidApp generates a base Application); Leakcanary installs itself via a provider.

Analogy. The opening checklist of a restaurant: whatever you add to the checklist delays opening time for every customer.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing onTerminate is called in production.
  • Putting disk or network work in Application.onCreate.
  • Forgetting each process runs its own Application.onCreate.

notes.title: ContentProvider auto-init and App Startup
notes.html:
The idea. Many libraries start themselves by hiding a tiny ContentProvider in their manifest, because providers run automatically at process start. This is convenient but every one adds startup cost.

Mechanism. A provider with android:authorities="${applicationId}.initprovider" is instantiated and its onCreate runs before Application.onCreate. Each costs a few milliseconds plus reflection and class loading; with 10 libraries it can be 50 to 150 ms on a mid-range phone. Jetpack App Startup (androidx.startup:startup-runtime) replaces many providers with a single InitializationProvider that runs Initializer<T> classes in dependency order.

class AnalyticsInitializer : Initializer<Analytics> {
    override fun create(context: Context) = Analytics.init(context)
    override fun dependencies() = listOf(LoggerInitializer::class.java)
}

To control it, remove an auto-initialiser with the manifest merger and initialise lazily:

<provider android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup" tools:node="merge">
    <meta-data android:name="androidx.work.WorkManagerInitializer" tools:node="remove"/>
</provider>

Alternatively tools:node="remove" the whole provider and call Library.init() on demand. WorkManager's on-demand initialisation (Configuration.Provider) and Firebase manual init are examples.

Industry examples. WorkManager, ProfileInstaller, Emoji2 and Lifecycle ProcessLifecycleOwner all use App Startup; LeakCanary uses a provider.

Analogy. Several delivery companies all dropping parcels at the front desk at opening time; App Startup is one receptionist sorting them in order.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing provider init happens after Application.onCreate. It happens before.
  • Removing a provider but not initialising the library, breaking it silently.
  • Ignoring cumulative startup cost from many SDK providers.

notes.title: Manifest merge
notes.html:
The idea. Your final manifest is not just the file you wrote. The build combines your manifest, every library's, product flavours and build types, then applies rules to settle conflicts.

Mechanism. The Manifest Merger tool merges in priority order: main source set, build-type and flavour overlays, then library (AAR) manifests, with the app winning conflicts. Markers: tools:node (merge, replace, remove, removeAll, strict), tools:attr, tools:replace="android:label", tools:remove, tools:selector="com.lib", tools:overrideLibrary (for minSdk mismatches). Placeholders: ${applicationId}, ${appAuthority}. View the result in Android Studio's "Merged Manifest" tab (with the origin of each line), or in app/build/outputs/logs/manifest-merger-*-report.txt. Typical failures: duplicated android:icon/android:label attributes, minSdk conflicts, a library adding android:allowBackup="true", usesCleartextTraffic, or extra permissions.

Industry examples. Ad SDK and analytics libraries often add permissions, receivers and providers; Firebase and Google Play services add a dozen components.

Analogy. Combining several people's shopping lists into one: you check the final list for things you never meant to buy.

Common interview traps.

  • Auditing only your own manifest file.
  • Using tools:replace for attributes that should be merged.
  • Ignoring merger warnings that point to a security-relevant component.

notes.title: Exported components, permissions and the merge security incident
notes.html:
The idea. Any component you export is a public door. A library can add such a door to your app without you knowing, and attackers will test it.

Mechanism. Rules: since API 31 android:exported is mandatory for components with intent filters; providers default to exported=false from targetSdk 17; use android:permission (and for providers readPermission, writePermission, grantUriPermissions, <path-permission>) to protect. Check the caller in code (Binder.getCallingUid, signature permission) for sensitive actions. Never trust extras of exported components, and avoid forwarding a received Intent to startActivity (intent redirection). android:allowBackup, android:debuggable, and usesCleartextTraffic also merge in.

Post-incident review (manifest merge and security). A security researcher reports that any app can read the user's tokens by calling an exported FileProvider/ContentProvider shipped by a third-party SDK. Timeline: SDK updated three weeks earlier; its AAR manifest added <provider exported="true">; nobody reviewed the merged manifest; no CI check. Root cause: missing merged-manifest review and defaults. Fixes: remove or override the provider (tools:node="remove"), rotate the token, publish a hotfix, add a CI script that parses the merged manifest and fails on new exported components or permissions not on an allow list, and add dependency update review.

Analogy. A contractor adds a back door to your shop and you only find out when someone walks in at night.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing exported="false" blocks all access (PendingIntents and same-UID still work).
  • Trusting intent extras from exported components.
  • Not diffing the merged manifest between releases.

notes.title: Package visibility on Android 11
notes.html:
The idea. Starting in Android 11 an app can no longer freely see which other apps are installed. This protects privacy.

Mechanism. For targetSdk 30+, PackageManager.getInstalledPackages, queryIntentActivities, getPackageInfo etc. return only apps that are "visible" to you: your own app, system apps that are always visible, apps that interact with you, and apps you declare in <queries>. Declaring:

<queries>
    <package android:name="com.whatsapp"/>
    <intent><action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/><data android:scheme="https"/></intent>
    <provider android:authorities="com.example.provider"/>
</queries>

QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES bypasses the filter but is restricted by Google Play to apps with a justified core function (antivirus, device management, launchers). Symptoms: getLaunchIntentForPackage returns null, resolveActivity returns null so "Open in Maps" buttons vanish, startActivity throws ActivityNotFoundException for an installed browser. Note: starting an explicit intent for a package still works even if the package isn't visible, but you can't verify it exists. Use ACTION_VIEW intents rather than checking for packages when possible.

Industry examples. Payment apps (Google Pay/UPI intent flows in Indian apps: Paytm, PhonePe, BHIM) declare <queries> for UPI intents so they can list UPI apps; sharing flows rely on the system chooser, which needs no visibility.

Analogy. Before, you could read the guest register of every house on the street; now you only see the houses you were introduced to.

Common interview traps.

  • Bumping targetSdk to 30 and seeing "app not installed" in features that use getInstalledPackages.
  • Using QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES casually (Play rejection).
  • Believing <queries> affects the ability to start an explicit intent.

notes.title: Resource qualifiers and resolution
notes.html:
The idea. One resource name can have many versions (for example values-hi, layout-sw600dp, drawable-night), and Android chooses the best match for the current phone state.

Mechanism. Qualifiers are appended to folder names in a fixed order: MCC/MNC, language/region (en-rIN, BCP 47 b+sr+Latn), layout direction (ldrtl), smallest width (sw600dp), available width/height (w720dp, h), screen size, aspect, orientation, UI mode, night mode (night), density (xxhdpi), touch type, keyboard, API level (v31). Resolution (simplified):

1. Remove folders that contradict the device configuration.
2. Take the qualifier highest in the precedence list that any remaining folder uses.
3. Keep the folders that have it; discard those that do not.
4. Repeat for the next qualifier until one folder remains.

Density is special: the system prefers scaling a bitmap down from a higher density rather than scaling up; vectors avoid this. API qualifiers (for example values-v31) let you ship version-specific themes. Compose uses WindowSizeClass for layout adaptation rather than relying on qualifiers. Qualifier changes cause a configuration change, which recreates the Activity unless handled with android:configChanges.

Industry examples. Material theme overlays use values-night, values-v31 for dynamic colours; apps use layout-sw600dp for tablet master/detail; drawable-nodpi for large background images to avoid scaling.

Analogy. Ordering clothes: filter by size first (most important), then colour, then style, until one item is left.

Common interview traps.

  • Placing qualifiers in the wrong order, so the folder is silently ignored (the build tool warns for some).
  • Putting a big photo into drawable (treated as mdpi, upscaled, memory explosion); use drawable-nodpi or drawable-xxhdpi.
  • Forgetting a default (non-qualified) resource, causing Resources.NotFoundException on some configurations.

notes.title: Locale resolution and fallback
notes.html:
The idea. When the user's language list is [Hindi, English], Android tries each in order and uses the first language your app has strings for. If you have none, it falls back to your default values/.

Mechanism. Since Android 7 (API 24) users have an ordered locale list; resources are resolved with a locale-matching algorithm that tries the user's locales in order and uses parent locales (en-rIN falls back to en, then default). The default res/values must contain every string (there is no inherited translation fallback beyond locale parents). Lint complains about MissingTranslation. resConfigs/resourceConfigurations in Gradle (and now androidResources { localeFilters }) strips other languages from the APK. Android 13 per-app language: locales_config.xml and AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales. Script and regional pitfalls: Hindi hi, Hinglish isn't a locale; Chinese zh-rCN vs zh-rTW or b+zh+Hans; legacy codes (iw to he, in to id, ji to yi) changed in Java but Android resource folders still use iw/in in older tooling (confirm the tool version). Locale.getDefault() returns the first locale of the list; LocaleList.getAdjustedDefault() returns all.

Spot-the-bug (locale override). The code:

val config = resources.configuration
config.setLocale(Locale("fr"))
resources.updateConfiguration(config, resources.displayMetrics)   // deprecated, global side effects

Problems: updateConfiguration is deprecated and modifies shared Resources, leaks into other contexts, is not applied to the Application context, resets on configuration change (rotation), ignores AppCompat's own handling, and is overridden by the Android 13 per-app locale. Fix: use AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags("fr")) (AppCompat 1.6+) or a wrapped context via createConfigurationContext in attachBaseContext; persist the choice; for non-Activity text use a locale-aware context.

Industry examples. Indian apps (Paytm, Swiggy, Hotstar, ShareChat) ship many regional languages; Facebook and WhatsApp use the system list with an in-app override.

Analogy. A menu with languages in your preference order; if the restaurant has no Hindi menu it tries English, and as a last resort uses its house language.

Common interview traps.

  • Using updateConfiguration and wondering why the language resets on rotation.
  • Not providing all strings in the default folder.
  • Treating Locale.getDefault() as the full preference list.

notes.title: Configuration, night mode and insets
notes.html:
The idea. The device state (orientation, font size, dark mode, language, window size, system bars) is called the Configuration. When it changes, Android normally destroys and recreates your Activity so every resource is re-picked.

Mechanism. Configuration fields: orientation, uiMode (night mask), fontScale, locales, densityDpi, screenWidthDp, smallestScreenWidthDp, screenLayout. A change triggers Activity.onConfigurationChanged only if you list it in android:configChanges; otherwise the Activity is recreated and ViewModels survive. Night mode: AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode(MODE_NIGHT_YES/NO/FOLLOW_SYSTEM) recreates Activities; values-night, drawable-night, Theme.Material3.DayNight; Compose uses isSystemInDarkTheme(). Context theming: ContextThemeWrapper or the Application context have the system night state, not the Activity's forced state, which can differ (Activity overrides via AppCompat's applyOverrideConfiguration). Insets: WindowInsetsCompat for status bar, navigation bar, cutout, IME; from Android 15 edge-to-edge is enforced for targetSdk 35. Foldables and multi-window (Android 12L, 16) change window size without orientation change; use WindowMetricsCalculator and window size classes.

Production incident (night mode context theming). Some views in a dialog showed dark text on a dark background only when the user toggled dark mode inside the app: the dialog was built with the Application context, which carries the system night state, while the Activity forced night via AppCompat. Fix: build dialogs and inflaters with the Activity context (LayoutInflater.from(activity)), pass the themed context into custom view factories, and test both forced modes.

Industry examples. Instagram, Twitter/X and WhatsApp offer in-app theme toggles layered on the system; YouTube and Gmail use DayNight.

Analogy. Changing the room's lighting: the whole room is re-set (recreated) unless you tell the staff you will adjust the lamps yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Using configChanges to avoid fixing state restoration.
  • Taking colours from the Application context after an in-app theme override.
  • Hard-coding system bar heights instead of using insets.

notes.title: Context leaks
notes.html:
The idea. A leak happens when something long-lived keeps a reference to something short-lived (an Activity), so the Activity's views and bitmaps can never be freed.

Mechanism. The GC cannot reclaim an Activity that is reachable from a GC root (static field, singleton, thread, running coroutine on a global scope, registered listener). An Activity holds its whole view tree, so a single leak may retain several MB.

Spot-the-bug.

object Analytics {
    lateinit var ctx: Context            // set from Activity: Analytics.ctx = this
}
class Repo(private val context: Context) // singleton created with an Activity
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    companion object { var lastToast: TextView? = null }   // static view
    // Handler().postDelayed({ binding.x.text = ... }, 60_000)  // lambda keeps Activity
}

Typical leaks: static Context or View, singletons given an Activity, anonymous inner classes/handlers, AsyncTask, unregistered listeners/receivers, GlobalScope jobs capturing this, ViewBinding kept in a Fragment after onDestroyView, LiveData.observeForever. Detect with LeakCanary (shows the leak trace "GC Root: static field ... -> Activity.mDestroyed = true"), the Android Studio memory profiler heap dump (look for multiple instances of the Activity), and StrictMode.setVmPolicy(detectActivityLeaks()). Fix: pass applicationContext, use lifecycle-aware components (lifecycleScope, viewLifecycleOwner), clear references in onDestroyView, use WeakReference only as a last resort.

Industry examples. LeakCanary found leaks in AOSP itself; Square and Uber report using it in CI instrumentation tests with LeakAssertions.

Analogy. A guest who checked out, but their name is still pinned to the only key in the front-desk drawer, so the room can never be cleaned and reused.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing WeakReference is the proper fix rather than lifetime alignment.
  • Assuming rotation leaks only matter on old phones; repeated rotations OOM low-RAM devices.
  • Storing Activity.applicationContext and thinking it is a leak; it is safe.

notes.title: Application startup cost
notes.html:
The idea. Everything you initialise in the Application, in ContentProviders and in the first Activity delays the moment the user sees something. Measure first, then delay what is not needed.

Cost/perf optimization worked example. Cold start 2.4 s (p90) on a mid-range device. Perfetto/System Tracing and Android Studio's startup profile show: Firebase + Crashlytics + Analytics + Ads init 380 ms, Dagger graph creation 220 ms, Room open + migration check 160 ms, a 150 ms JSON parse on the main thread, SharedPreferences read of 30 files 100 ms. Plan: (1) classify each initialiser as needed-for-first-frame, needed-soon, or lazy; (2) move non-first-frame work to a background thread or App Startup with explicit dependencies; (3) lazy Dagger/Hilt providers (Lazy<T>, Provider<T>), and Koin by lazy; (4) defer ad/analytics SDKs until after first frame (Choreographer post-frame or ProcessLifecycleOwner); (5) add Baseline Profiles (Jetpack Macrobenchmark) to precompile startup classes, often 20 to 30 percent faster; (6) track reportFullyDrawn(), Play vitals cold start (bad above ~5 s) and Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric in CI to prevent regressions. Result: 1.6 s.

Industry examples. Instagram, Facebook and Twitter published startup work using lazy initialisation and Baseline Profiles; Google's "App startup time" guidance names cold (>5 s bad), warm (>2 s) and hot (>1.5 s) vitals thresholds.

Analogy. Opening a shop: put out the sign and open the till first; stock the back shelves after customers are served.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising without measuring (guessing).
  • Moving work to a background thread but then blocking on it from the main thread.
  • Forgetting multi-process Application initialisation.

notes.title: App bundles, dynamic delivery and language splits
notes.html:
The idea. Instead of one giant APK for every phone, you upload an Android App Bundle (AAB) and Google Play builds small APKs tailored to each device (language, screen density, CPU architecture).

Mechanism. Play generates a base APK plus configuration splits: config.arm64_v8a, config.xxhdpi, config.hi (language), and optional dynamic feature modules (install-time, on-demand via Play Feature Delivery, or conditional). On-device the installer installs several APKs as one app (split APKs, PackageInstaller sessions). Downloads are typically about 15 percent smaller or more. Limits: base size caps (200 MB compressed download for the AAB; asset packs separate), dynamic feature modules need SplitCompat.install() in attachBaseContext for resources and code access, and SplitInstallManager for requests. Testing: bundletool build-apks --connected-device and install-apks, internal app sharing; bundletool also checks sizes. Excluding splits: bundle { language { enableSplit = false } } forces all languages into the base.

Production incident (language splits). After moving to AAB, some users who changed the system language after installing saw English even though Hindi strings existed. Reason: Play installed only the language splits that matched the user's locale list at install time; when the user later added Hindi, the Play Store downloads the missing language split in the background, but offline or on restricted devices it did not arrive, so the app fell back to default. In-app language switching made it worse: the app's own picker offered Tamil, but the Tamil split was missing, so the picker had no effect. Fixes: disable language splits (enableSplit = false) for apps with an in-app language picker, or use Play Feature Delivery SplitInstallRequest.addLanguage(Locale) to request the language and wait for INSTALLED before applying; use SplitCompat; monitor by logging the AppCompatDelegate locale vs resolved locale; and verify with bundletool --device-spec for several locales. Also, on device-sensitive SDKs, check that a library using assets isn't placed in an on-demand module that wasn't installed.

Industry examples. Netflix, Uber and Spotify use AABs with feature modules; games use asset packs (Play Asset Delivery) for large textures; apps with in-app language switchers (Duolingo, Paytm) disable language splits or request them.

Analogy. A tailor-made lunchbox for each pupil, with extra dishes delivered later on request; if you change diet mid-week and the delivery is late, you eat the default meal.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing an AAB can be installed directly on a device (it cannot).
  • Forgetting SplitCompat in feature modules.
  • Not testing with bundletool and a changed locale.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Context is the app's handle to the system: Application lives for the process, Activity for the screen; choose the shortest-lived context that works and never store an Activity in something long-lived.
  • ContextWrapper and attachBaseContext are the hooks to change locale, theme and font; the Application's onCreate is the heaviest, earliest shared place and runs once per process, after ContentProviders.
  • ContentProvider auto-init and App Startup add startup cost; control with tools:node="remove" and lazy init.
  • The merged manifest is the one that ships: audit exported components, permissions, allowBackup and cleartext flags after every dependency change.
  • Android 11 package visibility needs <queries>; QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES is restricted.
  • Resource qualifiers resolve by precedence order; locales fall back by parents then default; use AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales, not updateConfiguration.
  • Configuration changes recreate Activities; night mode and locale can differ between the Application and the Activity context.
  • AABs split by language, density and ABI; language splits plus in-app language pickers need care.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly is a Context in Android, and what are the different kinds of Context you get in an app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Context is everywhere, and most leaks, theming bugs and BadTokenExceptions trace back to using the wrong one. They want to see if you know it is a class hierarchy with different capabilities, not a magic handle.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Context is the abstract gateway to the app environment: resources, assets, files, system services, starting components. ContextImpl is the real implementation; everything else wraps it. The Application context lives as long as the process and has no UI theme. Activity is a ContextThemeWrapper, so it carries a theme and can show windows. Service is a plain ContextWrapper without UI theme. Choosing between them is about lifetime and UI capability."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Context is an abstract class. The framework creates one ContextImpl per Application, Activity, Service and so on, and each of those classes wraps its ContextImpl as mBase.

Context (abstract)
 +-- ContextImpl            (the real work: resources, services, files, intents)
 +-- ContextWrapper         (delegates everything to mBase, i.e. getBaseContext())
      +-- Application       (process lifetime, no UI theme from manifest activity)
      +-- Service           (service lifetime, no UI theme)
      +-- ContextThemeWrapper  (adds a Theme + optional override Configuration)
           +-- Activity     (activity lifetime, has window token, theme from manifest)
Capability Application Service Activity
Lifetime process until destroyed until destroyed (recreated on config change)
Inflate with activity theme no (app theme only) no yes
Show Dialog / add window with app token no (BadTokenException) no yes
startActivity only with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK same yes
Safe to hold in a singleton yes no never

Other Context sources: ContentProvider.getContext() (the application's base context), BroadcastReceiver.onReceive(context) (a restricted context: registerReceiver(null...) ok, bindService not allowed; its getApplicationContext() is the Application), and createWindowContext (API 30) for UI outside an Activity, e.g. overlays.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Example(private val appContext: Context) { // store applicationContext only
    fun cacheDir() = appContext.cacheDir
}
// in an Activity
Example(applicationContext)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking getApplicationContext() and this are interchangeable.
  • Inflating layouts with the Application context and losing theme attributes (wrong colors, ?attr/... unresolved).
  • Believing a BroadcastReceiver's context is an Activity-like context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does getBaseContext() return in an Activity? → The wrapped ContextImpl, not the Activity itself.
  2. Can you startActivity from the Application context? → Yes with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK; without it you get AndroidRuntimeException: Calling startActivity() from outside of an Activity context.
  3. Why does getDisplay() throw on Application context at API 30+? → It is not associated with a display; Context.getDisplay() requires a visual context (Activity, or createWindowContext/createDisplayContext). StrictMode flags incorrectContextUse violations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Application context for long-lived things, Activity context for UI." Senior: explains the ContextWrapper chain, that visual-ness (token, display, theme) is what differs, and mentions window/display contexts on API 30+.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Overlay features built with the Application context crashed on Android 11 once strict visual-context checks arrived; moving to createWindowContext fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: When should I use the Activity context and when the Application context? Give concrete cases of each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quick filter. A weak candidate answers "Application always, to avoid leaks". A good one answers per use case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Anything that touches UI or themes uses the Activity context: inflating views, creating Dialogs, resolving theme attributes, startActivity without flags. Anything that outlives the screen, like a singleton, repository, Room/WorkManager/Retrofit setup, takes the Application context. So the rule is: match the context to the lifetime of the thing holding it, and use Activity only for what needs UI."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Dialog / AlertDialog / PopupWindow / Toast-with-custom-view: needs a window token (Activity). AlertDialog.Builder(applicationContext) throws WindowManager$BadTokenException: Unable to add window -- token null is not for an application.
  • Layout inflation: LayoutInflater.from(applicationContext) resolves styles against the application theme, ignoring the activity's theme (Material3 attributes, night overrides). Views render with wrong colors but do not crash, which is why it ships.
  • Resource lookups with ?attr: only Activity (or a ContextThemeWrapper) knows the active theme.
  • Singletons, DBs, DataStore, WorkManager, analytics: Application context. Holding an Activity here leaks the whole view hierarchy.
  • Navigation: startActivity from Application context requires FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK, which changes back-stack behavior. Prefer Activity context.
  • Compose: use LocalContext.current (the Activity or ContextWrapper over it) and unwrap with a ContextWrapper loop when you need the Activity.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// correct: DI graph gets application context
@Provides @Singleton
fun db(@ApplicationContext ctx: Context) =
    Room.databaseBuilder(ctx, AppDb::class.java, "app.db").build()

// correct: dialog gets the Activity
MaterialAlertDialogBuilder(this).setTitle("Delete?").show()

// unwrap in Compose helper
tailrec fun Context.findActivity(): Activity? = when (this) {
    is Activity -> this
    is ContextWrapper -> baseContext.findActivity()
    else -> null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing this (Activity) into a singleton "just to get resources".
  • Casting LocalContext.current as Activity (can be a ContextWrapper, crashes in some hosts).
  • Using the Application context to inflate dialog content and wondering why dark theme is wrong.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A repository needs a string resource. What do you do? → Inject Application context, or better, have the UI layer resolve strings (a UiText wrapper), so the data layer stays locale/theme agnostic.
  2. Is the Application context ever wrong for resources? → Yes for theme-dependent and per-activity configuration overrides (see the night mode and locale questions).
  3. How do you detect wrong-context usage early? → StrictMode detectIncorrectContextUse() (API 30+) and detectLeakedClosableObjects, plus LeakCanary for held Activities.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE gives the two-bucket rule. Senior adds that data layers should not need a Context at all for strings, and that the Application context is not "safe for everything" (theme, locale override, window).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Wrong inflater context caused a dark-mode-only unreadable bottom sheet that QA missed on light-theme devices.

questions.promptHtml: What is attachBaseContext used for, and how does ContextWrapper let you override locale or configuration for an Activity?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that Activity's resources can be replaced by wrapping the base context, the mechanism behind in-app language switching, SplitCompat and AppCompat night mode.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "attachBaseContext(newBase) is called by the framework before onCreate hands the component its ContextImpl. Since Activity is a ContextWrapper, I can override it and pass a wrapped context built with createConfigurationContext(config), so everything the Activity reads from resources uses my locale or font scale. It must be set before onCreate because views inflate from it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity creation: ActivityThread.performLaunchActivity creates a ContextImpl, instantiates the Activity, calls activity.attach(context, ...) which calls attachBaseContext(context). Whatever you pass to super.attachBaseContext becomes mBase.

createConfigurationContext(Configuration) returns a new ContextImpl sharing the package info but with different Resources (cached by a ResourcesKey). Resource lookups now use the override configuration.

Gotchas:

  • The override only affects that wrapped context. applicationContext, Services, notifications and other Activities are untouched unless wrapped too.
  • On config change (rotation), Activity is re-attached with a fresh base, so your override runs again. Your locale must come from persisted state.
  • AppCompat does the same: AppCompatDelegate.attachBaseContext2 applies night mode and locale through applyOverrideConfiguration. If you also wrap, call super appropriately or you get "lost" night mode; hence the known recommended pattern is to use AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales on AppCompat 1.6+ instead of hand-rolled wrapping.
  • WebView (some versions) and Application configuration changes could reset locale on an Activity resume (applyOverrideConfiguration order matters).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun attachBaseContext(newBase: Context) {
    val tag = LocalePrefs.read(newBase) // e.g. "hi-IN"
    val cfg = Configuration(newBase.resources.configuration).apply {
        setLocales(LocaleList(Locale.forLanguageTag(tag)))
    }
    super.attachBaseContext(newBase.createConfigurationContext(cfg))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using the deprecated resources.updateConfiguration(...): mutates shared Resources, leaks to other screens and is deprecated since API 25.
  • Forgetting to apply the same wrapping in Services/Application, so notifications show the system language.
  • Reading prefs from a Context before attachBaseContext finishes (use newBase, not this).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not do it in onCreate? → Too late; setContentView and many lookups can already use the old resources, and mBase is final in effect.
  2. Modern replacement? → AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales() (AppCompat 1.6.0+), and LocaleManager.setApplicationLocales on API 33+.
  3. What happens to a Compose app? → LocalConfiguration comes from the Activity's resources, so the wrapper works, but you must recreate the Activity after changing locale.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "override attachBaseContext to change language." Senior: explains the wrapper chain, scoping limits, deprecated updateConfiguration, and prefers platform per-app language APIs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hand-rolled locale wrapper fixed screens but left push notifications and Service strings in the system language for 100% of Hindi-selected users.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Application class for, when is onCreate called, and what should (and should not) go in it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cold-start cost and process-lifecycle misconceptions show up here. Seniors guard Application.onCreate because every component start pays for it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "One Application instance exists per process, created before any Activity, Service, Receiver or Provider code runs, except providers' onCreate, which runs before Application.onCreate. It's the right place for process-wide singletons and light init like DI graph setup or crash reporting. It's the wrong place for disk, network or SDK-heavy work, because it runs on the main thread on every cold start, including cold starts caused by a broadcast or a WorkManager job."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Order inside a new process (ActivityThread.handleBindApplication):

Application constructor
  -> attachBaseContext(base)        (Application is a ContextWrapper)
  -> ContentProvider.onCreate() x N (all providers declared in this process)
  -> Application.onCreate()
  -> then the component that triggered start (Activity/Service/Receiver)

Key facts:

  • Application is not guaranteed to live forever: after process death the process is recreated with a new Application, and all your static state is gone. This is the root of "works until backgrounded" bugs.
  • Application.onCreate runs for any component start, so a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver wakes the whole init path.
  • Multi-process apps (android:process) create one Application per process; guard with Application.getProcessName() (API 28) and skip heavy init in :remote processes.
  • onTrimMemory, onLowMemory, ComponentCallbacks2 and registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks live here.
  • Static fields set in Application survive configuration changes but not process death. Do not treat Application as a persistence layer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        if (getProcessName() != packageName) return // skip :sync, :push processes
        CrashReporter.init(this)         // cheap, must be early
        // heavy SDKs: lazy / background / App Startup
    }
}

Manifest: <application android:name=".App" ...>.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing synchronous SharedPreferences/IO and 10 SDK inits in onCreate.
  • Using it as a global state bag (App.currentUser), then NPE after process death.
  • Forgetting the manifest android:name after renaming.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a component run before Application.onCreate? → Yes, ContentProvider onCreate, and attachBaseContext.
  2. Is Application.onTerminate reliable? → No, it's only called in emulated environments, never on real devices.
  3. How do you measure Application init cost? → Perfetto/Trace.beginSection, Macrobenchmark StartupMode.COLD, adb shell am start -W (TotalTime) and Android vitals cold start.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "initialize libraries there." Senior: init order incl. providers, multi-process duplication, process-death amnesia, and a rule that nothing blocking goes in.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A silent push receiver triggered full SDK init for 5M daily wakeups, blowing battery stats until init was made lazy.

questions.promptHtml: Why do many SDKs initialize through a ContentProvider, and how does Jetpack App Startup change that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of hidden cold-start cost and the init order, plus how to control it using manifest merging.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Providers are instantiated by the system at process start before Application.onCreate, with a Context, so libraries use them as an auto-init hook without asking you to touch your Application. The cost: each provider costs main-thread time on every cold start, and you can't control the order. App Startup replaces N providers with one InitializationProvider that runs Initializers in dependency order, and you can disable or defer any initializer by removing its meta-data node in the manifest."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Providers: installContentProviders runs for all non-multiprocess-skipped providers in the process, ordered by initOrder (android:initOrder, higher first) and not very deterministically otherwise. Each costs class load + instantiate + onCreate, roughly 1-30 ms each on mid-range devices; 10 SDKs add up to hundreds of ms.
  • App Startup (androidx.startup:startup-runtime, 1.1.1 stable; 1.2.0 later): one androidx.startup.InitializationProvider (authority ${applicationId}.androidx-startup). Libraries declare <meta-data android:name="com.x.MyInitializer" android:value="androidx.startup" /> inside it; manifest merging gathers them. Initializer<T>.create(context) returns the component; dependencies() returns other initializers to run first.
  • Control: remove with tools:node="remove" and call AppInitializer.getInstance(ctx).initializeComponent(MyInitializer::class.java) later (lazy init).
  • Third-party SDK providers (not App Startup) can also be removed via tools:node="remove" on the <provider>, then init manually. Check the SDK docs; some require the provider's side effects.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<!-- disable WorkManager's auto init and initialize on demand (WorkManager 2.6+) -->
<provider
    android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup"
    android:exported="false"
    tools:node="merge">
    <meta-data
        android:name="androidx.work.WorkManagerInitializer"
        android:value="androidx.startup"
        tools:node="remove" />
</provider>

Then implement Configuration.Provider in Application.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Removing the initializer but never initializing: silent feature failure (analytics never starts).
  • Assuming Application.onCreate runs first, then reading state in a provider that's not initialized.
  • Adding App Startup for a single initializer and measuring no gain.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a provider run in each process? → Yes, per process unless android:process places it in a specific one.
  2. How do you find providers costing startup? → Perfetto slices ActivityThread.installProvider/contentProviderCreate, or merged manifest review.
  3. Can a provider start before Hilt/Dagger is ready? → Yes; do not depend on the graph in provider code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "App Startup helps cold start." Senior: explains ordering, merge-based opt-out, lazy init, and audits third-party providers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Removing three analytics providers and initializing them after first frame cut p50 cold start by ~140 ms in a mid-range cohort.

questions.promptHtml: How does the manifest merger work, in which priority order, and how do you resolve conflicts with tools: markers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Libraries silently add permissions, components and attributes. Seniors audit the merged manifest.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "AGP merges manifests by priority: the app's variant manifests (buildType, flavors) override the main manifest, which overrides library and AAR manifests. Elements merge by key (name, for components), attributes conflict when values differ. I resolve conflicts with tools:replace, tools:remove, tools:node markers in my manifest, and I always read the Merged Manifest tab and the merge report before release."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Priority (highest first): build-type manifest > flavor manifests > main manifest > libraries (in dependency order) . Elements with the same key (e.g. <activity android:name>) are merged by attribute; conflicting attribute values fail the build with Attribute application@allowBackup value=(true) from ... is also present at ... Suggestion: add 'tools:replace="android:allowBackup"'.

Marker Effect
tools:node="merge" default
tools:node="replace" replace the lower-priority element entirely
tools:node="remove" drop that element from the result
tools:node="removeAll" drop all same-type elements
tools:node="strict" fail if lower-priority differs
tools:replace="a,b" / tools:remove="a" per-attribute
tools:selector="com.lib" target a specific library's contribution

Placeholders ${applicationId} and manifest placeholders from Gradle manifestPlaceholders. Inspect with Android Studio "Merged Manifest" tab, or app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests/<variant>/ and outputs/logs/manifest-merger-<variant>-report.txt, which says which library contributed which line.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<!-- drop a permission some SDK adds -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_PHONE_STATE"
    tools:node="remove" />
<!-- resolve attribute conflict -->
<application android:allowBackup="false"
    tools:replace="android:allowBackup" />

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• tools:node="remove" on a permission another module truly needs, causing a runtime SecurityException.
  • Not declaring the xmlns:tools namespace.
  • Only checking the debug merged manifest when release adds different library flavors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you drop a transitive component? → tools:node="remove" with the exact android:name.
  2. Where does minSdk mismatch show? → Merge error uses-sdk:minSdkVersion X cannot be smaller than version Y declared in library; fix with tools:overrideLibrary only if you verified the library works.
  3. Do ProGuard rules merge the same way? → No; consumer rules are separate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use tools:replace when the build errors." Senior: reads the merge report, treats it as a security/compliance surface, and enforces a CI diff of the merged manifest.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A new ad SDK added AD_ID and an exported receiver; caught only because CI diffed the merged release manifest.

questions.promptHtml: Explain android:exported, component permissions and the API 31 changes. How do you secure an exported component?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common security question. Wrongly exported components are a top vulnerability class.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "exported=true lets other apps start or bind the component. Since targetSdk 31 you must set android:exported explicitly on any component with an intent-filter, else the app fails to install/parse. Default for providers with targetSdk 17+ is false. To secure an exported component I either need it exported for a reason, then guard with a signature-level permission and validate every incoming Intent, or I don't export it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Without intent-filter: default exported=false (components) and an explicit true makes them public.
  • With an intent-filter on targetSdk 31+: compile/install error Targets S+ ... android:exported needs to be explicitly specified for element <activity>.
  • Launcher activity must be exported=true.
  • android:permission="com.app.PERM" on a component requires callers to hold it. Define it with <permission android:name=... android:protectionLevel="signature"/> so only apps signed with your key qualify.
  • Provider: android:readPermission / writePermission, grantUriPermissions for temporary per-URI grants (FileProvider pattern).
  • Receivers registered at runtime (API 33+, required for apps targeting 34): registerReceiver(r, filter, RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED); targeting U with neither flag throws SecurityException for non-system broadcasts.
  • PendingIntent mutability and intent redirection are covered in the Intents chunk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<permission android:name="com.example.permission.PARTNER_API"
    android:protectionLevel="signature" />

<service android:name=".PartnerService"
    android:exported="true"
    android:permission="com.example.permission.PARTNER_API">
    <intent-filter><action android:name="com.example.PARTNER" /></intent-filter>
</service>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting exported=true to "make deep links work" on every Activity.
  • Trusting extras from exported components (path traversal, intent redirection).
  • Using normal protection level and assuming that means private.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does exported=false block the system? → No: the same UID, the system and root can still start it.
  2. How do you verify exposure? → aapt2 dump xmltree, merged manifest, adb shell dumpsys package <pkg>, Play pre-launch/security scan, drozer.
  3. Why is permission-name squatting a risk? → If another app installs first and defines your permission name, protection falls to the first definer; use signature-level plus your own naming.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE knows the flag. Senior treats exported surface as an API: minimal, permission-guarded, input-validated, audited in CI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An exported debug-only ProxyActivity shipped to release and allowed another app to open arbitrary screens as logged-in user.

questions.promptHtml: What changed in Android 11 for package visibility, and how do <queries> work?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production breakage with silent null results; many "intent not resolving on Android 11" bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "From API 30, with targetSdk 30+, PackageManager only returns apps that are auto-visible or that I declare under <queries>. Without it, resolveActivity returns null and getPackageInfo throws NameNotFoundException even though the app is installed. I declare the specific package, intent filter, or provider authority I need; QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES is restricted by Play policy."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Auto-visible: your own app, certain system packages, apps that started your Activity via startActivityForResult, the app that holds a content provider you're accessing via URI grant, and apps already interacting in-session.

<queries>
    <package android:name="com.whatsapp" />
    <intent>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <data android:scheme="https" />
    </intent>
    <provider android:authorities="com.partner.provider" />
</queries>

Behaviors:

  • startActivity on an implicit intent still launches the handler even if not visible; the query is what returns empty, but startActivity for a non-visible target can throw ActivityNotFoundException in some flows. The safe pattern is try { startActivity } catch (ActivityNotFoundException).
  • Runtime: filtered queryIntentActivities/getInstalledApplications return only visible apps (no exception, just fewer).
  • For browsers: declare an https VIEW intent in <queries> to resolve a browser for Custom Tabs (CustomTabsClient.getPackageName).
  • AGP 4.1+ understands <queries>; older AGP merges poorly.
  • Behavior depends on targetSdk, not just OS, but device OS must be 11+.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing on emulator with the browser auto-visible and shipping a broken feature to Android 11+ real devices.
  • Asking QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES for a convenience feature; Play review rejects.
  • Checking resolveActivity(...) != null as a guard but not declaring <queries>, so the feature is always hidden.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check for app installed on 11+? → getPackageInfo in try/catch after <queries><package/></queries>.
  2. Library SDK needs visibility? → It should add <queries> in its own manifest; they merge into yours.
  3. Does it affect Intent.createChooser? → The chooser works without visibility, since the system resolves.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "add queries". Senior: knows silent-failure semantics, auto-visible set, Play policy, and tests on API 30+ devices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Open in UPI app" feature disappeared on Android 11+ because the resolve check silently returned empty.

questions.promptHtml: How does Android pick a resource when multiple qualified versions exist (values-night, drawable-xhdpi, layout-sw600dp, values-v31)? Walk me through the resolution algorithm.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many "wrong layout/drawable on some device" bugs come from not knowing the precedence table and the elimination algorithm.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The system first throws away every directory that contradicts the current device configuration. Then it walks the qualifier precedence table from the top (MCC, MNC, locale, layout direction, smallestWidth, available width/height, screen size, ratio, orientation, UI mode, night mode, density, ... platform version). At the first qualifier that any remaining directory uses, it keeps only the directories having it. It repeats until one directory remains. Density is special: no exact match scales the best neighbour."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Precedence (high to low, abridged): MCC/MNC > locale > layout direction > swNNNdp > wNNNdp > hNNNdp > size > long/notlong > round > orientation > UI mode > night > density > touch/keyboard/nav > API level (vNN).

Example. Device: Hindi locale, sw411dp, night, xxhdpi, API 34. Candidates for string/title with dirs values, values-hi, values-night, values-sw600dp:

  1. Drop values-sw600dp (contradicts, 411 < 600).
  2. Remaining qualifiers present: locale (hi) is the highest in the table, so keep only values-hi. values-night is lost even though it matches, because locale outranks night.

So qualifiers don't combine unless they are in the same directory name (values-hi-night), and they must be written in precedence order (values-hi-night, not values-night-hi) or aapt2 errors.

Density: exact match wins; with no exact match the system picks a better-than-needed bucket and scales down (preferring downscale over blurry upscale), with nodpi and anydpi special. Vector drawables sidestep this. -v31 only applies at API 31+ and is the standard way to ship version-specific styles/themes.

sw is the smallest dimension and rotation independent, w is the current available width, which changes with rotation, foldable posture and multi-window; so for tablet vs phone layouts use sw, for foldable/windowed use w or Window Size Classes (androidx.window).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
res/
  values/strings.xml
  values-hi/strings.xml           # Hindi
  values-night/colors.xml         # dark colors
  values-sw600dp/dimens.xml       # tablets
  values-v31/themes.xml           # Android 12+ attributes
  drawable-xxhdpi/ic.png
  drawable-anydpi-v26/ic.xml      # adaptive icon (API 26+)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrong order of qualifiers in directory name.
  • Expecting -night to override a locale-specific file.
  • Using layout-land and layout-sw600dp both and not knowing sw wins over orientation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which wins: layout-sw600dp or layout-land? → sw600dp (higher in the table).
  2. What is values-b+sr+Latn? → BCP-47 locale directory (API 21+).
  3. What if default values/ lacks a string present in values-hi? → Lint MissingDefaultResource; the app crashes with Resources$NotFoundException on other locales.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists qualifiers. Senior states the precedence/elimination algorithm and predicts an outcome for a tricky combination.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Tablet users got a phone layout after a refactor changed layout-large to layout-w600dp, which varies on rotation.

questions.promptHtml: How does Android resolve the locale for resources, what is the fallback chain, and how does per-app language (API 33) fit in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Localization bugs are a regular production issue, especially multilingual markets such as India.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Since API 24 the user has an ordered LocaleList. For each resource Android tries locale list entries in order against available qualifiers (language+region, then language), falling back to the default values/. Apps can override per app: API 33 LocaleManager.setApplicationLocales with a locales_config.xml declared in the manifest, and AppCompat 1.6+ backports it to older versions."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Configuration.getLocales() returns the list; Locale.getDefault() is just the first and is a JVM global that can be changed by libraries.
  • Matching: for en-GB the system tries values-en-rGB, then values-en, then values. Android 7+ also allows a later entry in the user's list to be chosen if the app has no match for the first, giving "Hindi then English" behavior instead of straight default.
  • Missing default strings are the common crash/embarrassment source: values/strings.xml is the ultimate fallback and must hold every key.
  • Per-app language (Android 13 / API 33): declare <application android:localeConfig="@xml/locales_config"> with <locale-config><locale android:name="hi-IN"/>...</locale-config>. With AGP 8.1+ you can set androidResources { generateLocaleConfig = true } and a resources.properties with unqualifiedResLocale=en-US. Users change it in system Settings > Apps > Language.
  • Pre-33: AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags("hi")) plus a manifest service AppLocalesMetadataHolderService with autoStoreLocales=true to persist.
  • Formatting (dates, numbers, plurals) uses Locale and ICU, not directory resolution; plural categories differ per language (quantity="few", many), so translation files need all required quantities.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// API 33+ native
getSystemService(LocaleManager::class.java).applicationLocales =
    LocaleList.forLanguageTags("hi-IN")

// all versions with AppCompat 1.6+
AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags("hi-IN"))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Locale.getDefault() for UI language decisions when the app has an override.
  • Missing default-locale strings; lint MissingTranslation ignored.
  • resourceConfigurations/resConfigs stripping locales that users do speak.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does changing app locale recreate the Activity? → Yes, the config changes; with AppCompat it recreates.
  2. How do you test a locale quickly? → adb shell cmd locale set-app-locales <pkg> --locales hi-IN (API 33+), or device settings; pseudolocales (en-XA, ar-XB) via pseudoLocalesEnabled true.
  3. How does this interact with app bundles? → Language config splits must be installed; see the bundle question.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "values-hi for Hindi". Senior knows the LocaleList fallback, the API 33 per-app APIs, plural/format differences, and RTL.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Marathi-and-English user saw Hindi in the app because list-based matching picked the next language the app supported.

questions.promptHtml: What does Resources.getConfiguration() contain, how does night mode actually get applied, and how does that differ between Application and Activity context? Where do window insets fit in?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know that Configuration is per-context state and that the Activity can override it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Configuration holds locales, uiMode (night bit, car/TV type), fontScale, orientation, screen size in dp, densityDpi. Each Resources object has its own copy. The system pushes changes to the process; an Activity without configChanges is recreated. AppCompat's night mode rewrites the Activity's override configuration, so the Activity sees night while the Application context may still see the system value. That mismatch is why using the Application context for colors is a bug."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• config.uiMode and Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_MASK == UI_MODE_NIGHT_YES tells night.
  • System dark theme change: ActivityThread.handleConfigurationChanged -> onConfigurationChanged for components that declared configChanges="uiMode", otherwise relaunch.
  • AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode(MODE_NIGHT_YES/NO/FOLLOW_SYSTEM) overrides per process; AppCompat applies it by calling applyOverrideConfiguration with a modified uiMode on the Activity's base. The Application context is unaffected, as are Services/notifications.
  • Theme: Theme.Material3.DayNight picks values-night colors via the Activity's configuration. Force dark (API 29) is for apps with no dark theme: android:forceDarkAllowed.
  • Compose: isSystemInDarkTheme() reads LocalConfiguration, so it follows the Activity override only if the Activity actually got the new uiMode.
  • Font scale from API 34 is non-linear above 1.0 up to 200%; use sp and test at 200%.
  • Insets: apps targeting SDK 35 on Android 15 get edge-to-edge enforced. Use enableEdgeToEdge() (activity 1.8+) and ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener / Compose Modifier.safeDrawingPadding(). They are delivered via the view hierarchy (WindowInsets), not Configuration, and also change independent of recreation. (Details in the window/UI chunks.)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val isNight = (resources.configuration.uiMode and
    Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_MASK) == Configuration.UI_MODE_NIGHT_YES

AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode(AppCompatDelegate.MODE_NIGHT_YES)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading applicationContext.resources.configuration to decide the theme.
  • Using configChanges="uiMode" without handling the callback, leaving stale colors.
  • Caching colors/drawables statically across theme changes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can recreation cause a flash/loss? → ViewModel survives, but unsaved UI state does not; use SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable.
  2. Per-app theme on Android 12+? → UiModeManager.setApplicationNightMode (API 31+) sets it at the platform level, while AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode works on all versions.
  3. Why is Resources.updateConfiguration bad? → Mutates shared state; deprecated.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "values-night". Senior: configuration is per Resources/context, AppCompat overrides it on the Activity only, and inset delivery is a separate channel.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An in-app dark toggle left notification icons and a widget in system theme for all users who differed from system settings.

questions.promptHtml: What is an Android App Bundle, how does Play build device-specific APKs from it, and what delivery options exist for dynamic feature modules?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Release and size trade-offs; also surfaces missing-resource bugs after language/density splits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "An AAB is a publishing format, not installable. Play generates split APKs per device: a base APK plus config splits for ABI, screen density and language, plus optional dynamic feature module splits. Smaller downloads, but behavior changes: only the languages and densities Play thinks the device needs are installed. Dynamic features can be install-time, on-demand, or conditional."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
app.aab -> bundletool/Play -> base.apk
                              config.arm64_v8a.apk
                              config.xxhdpi.apk
                              config.hi.apk
                              feature_x.apk (+ its config splits)
  • Required for new apps on Play since August 2021; limit 200 MB compressed download for base, with asset packs/features extending (Play Asset Delivery for large assets).
  • Delivery: install-time (bundled at install, includes onDemand=false), on-demand (SplitInstallManager.startInstall), conditional (device feature, country, API level).
  • Feature code is loaded via a split class loader; on-demand features need SplitCompat.install(this) (via SplitCompatApplication or in attachBaseContext) so resources/code are available to existing contexts. Activities opened from a split need SplitCompat.installActivity.
  • Tests: bundletool build-apks --connected-device or --local-testing, bundletool install-multi-apks. Internal App Sharing for real-device validation.
  • Gotchas: Resources.NotFoundException / ClassNotFoundException when split not installed; language splits (see the scenario below); reflection/Class.forName into feature module classes.
  • Dynamic feature modules vs plain library modules: the latter are always in base.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val manager = SplitInstallManagerFactory.create(context)
val req = SplitInstallRequest.newBuilder().addModule("feature_scan").build()
manager.startInstall(req)
    .addOnSuccessListener { sessionId -> /* observe listener */ }
    .addOnFailureListener { e -> /* retry/fallback UI */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing only with a universal APK, so split-only bugs reach production.
  • Starting the feature Activity before the install state is INSTALLED.
  • Ignoring the on-demand feature failure modes (no network, storage).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. APK vs AAB size difference? → Typically 15-30% smaller downloads, varies; measure with Play Console "download size".
  2. Can you ship outside Play with AAB? → Generate APKs via bundletool; no dynamic delivery.
  3. Alternative to dynamic features? → Instant Apps use a similar mechanism; many teams just use R8 and asset packs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "smaller app." Senior discusses split mechanics, test strategy, SplitCompat, and failure handling.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An on-demand scanner module crashed with ClassNotFound for users who tapped faster than the install completed.

questions.contextHtml:
Crash rate is fine, but OOM-killed sessions rose from 0.4% to 1.1% after release 8.3 on 2 GB RAM devices (about 38% of 900k DAU). LeakCanary in debug shows HomeActivity retained after back-press, leak trace: GC Root: static ImageLoader.instance -> ImageLoader.ctx -> HomeActivity. The relevant code:

object ImageLoader {
    lateinit var ctx: Context
    fun init(context: Context) { ctx = context }
    fun placeholder() = ctx.getDrawable(R.drawable.ph)
}
// HomeActivity.onCreate
ImageLoader.init(this)

A teammate says "just switch to a WeakReference".
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you fix it correctly, and how do you stop it recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WeakReference" or "set ctx = null in onDestroy". These hide the symptom, keep a nullable Context path, and leave other statics around.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the leak in release too (OOM kills are, not only debug)? Which devices? Is init called from other screens (different Activities leak each time)? Did 8.3 introduce this singleton or was it always there? Are there other statics holding views, e.g. Handler, callbacks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: ImageLoader.init(applicationContext). Ship via staged rollout; check OOM rate and Android vitals.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) static holds Activity (matches trace); (b) Bitmaps in an unbounded cache; (c) fragment view binding retained; (d) coroutine scope outliving the Activity. The trace points to (a), but I still check (b) because an OOM rise could have two causes (red herring: only the debug leak shows).
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary trace; Android Studio heap dump, filter HomeActivity instances after rotating three times; adb shell dumpsys meminfo <pkg> shows Activities: count rising; compare release vs previous with Perfetto memory counters.
  5. Root cause: A static (GC root) strongly references an Activity, so the Activity, its window, view tree and bitmaps stay reachable until process death. Every rotation leaks another instance.
  6. Fix: Short-term: application context. Long-term: inject @ApplicationContext through DI, remove lateinit var ctx global state, and if drawables need theme use the caller's context at call time, not stored.
class ImageLoader @Inject constructor(@ApplicationContext private val ctx: Context)
  1. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug and CI with Espresso rotation test (ActivityScenario.recreate() + assertNoLeaks), a lint/detekt rule banning Context static fields (StaticFieldLeak lint), and review checklist.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not WeakReference (nullability bugs, hides design flaw). Not largeHeap. Application context is fine here but is wrong for theme-dependent drawable resolution, so I verify the placeholder drawable is theme independent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the loader needs a themed drawable? → Pass the Activity context per call and do not retain it.
  • Does the Application context leak? → No, it lives as long as the process; it can still hold heavy objects you attach.
  • Would Hilt scoping change this? → @Singleton with @ApplicationContext is safe; injecting @ActivityContext into a singleton is the bug.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feed screen's rotation leaks were invisible for months because users rarely rotated, but a split-screen feature multiplied recreation and tipped the OOM rate overnight.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests WeakReference/largeHeap, cannot read a leak trace.
  • Hire: Application context fix, explains GC root, uses heap dump or LeakCanary.
  • Strong hire: also tests recreation in CI, bans static contexts via lint, separates theme-needing paths, and checks for a second OOM cause.

questions.contextHtml: Fintech app, 2M DAU, 55% on devices with 3-4 GB RAM. Android vitals reports cold start p90 at 3.4 s; Play's "excessive" threshold is 5 s (we are under it), but product wants p90 below 2.2 s. Application.onCreate is 410 ms on a Redmi-class device (Perfetto). Eight SDKs (analytics, crash, ads, attribution, chat, maps, payments, feature flags) each initialize in Application.onCreate, and three of them also add their own <provider>. Before onCreate even starts, Perfetto shows ~260 ms in installContentProviders. Home screen first frame at ~1.1 s after onCreate. A second red herring: a BOOT_COMPLETED receiver also triggers the same init.
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut cold start, in what order, and how do you prove it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move everything to a background thread." Some SDKs are not thread-safe or must run on main, ordering breaks (crash reporter after the first crash), and the provider cost is untouched.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which metric: TTID or TTFD (reportFullyDrawn)? Which cohort and which start type (cold vs warm)? Which SDKs are contractually required to start early (crash, consent)? Is there a Baseline Profile already? What does a headless launch (receiver/WorkManager) cost us?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed, not an outage. First step is measurement with a trace on a low-end device.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) provider auto-init, 260 ms; (b) serial SDK init on main, 410 ms; (c) no Baseline Profile, so the first screen runs in interpreter/JIT; (d) heavy first-screen work (DI graph, DB open, prefs). Red herring: network calls inside SDK init look slow but are async.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto with Trace.beginSection around each SDK; Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric with CompilationMode.None() vs Partial() (Baseline Profile); adb shell am start -W -S for TotalTime; StrictMode for disk reads on main; Android Studio Profiler system trace.
  5. Root cause: Everything is serial on the main thread before the first frame, and providers pay hidden cost for libraries that don't need to be ready until a later screen.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: remove the three SDK providers with tools:node="remove", init lazily via App Startup/on first use; defer ads/attribution/chat to after first frame (Looper.myQueue().addIdleHandler or a post-reportFullyDrawn coroutine on a background dispatcher).
    • Keep crash reporting and consent first.
    • Skip heavy init when launched by a receiver: lightweight path by checking the component starting the process is not a UI start.
    • Long-term: Baseline Profile + startup profile (dex layout), App Startup dependency graph, and an init budget policy.
class AdsInitializer : Initializer<Unit> {
    override fun create(context: Context) { Ads.init(context) }
    override fun dependencies() = listOf(ConsentInitializer::class.java)
}
  1. Prevention: Macrobenchmark in CI with regression thresholds (fail PR if p50 > +5%), a module-level init budget doc, review rule: new SDK init needs trace evidence.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blindly threading unknown SDKs; deferring ads init may lower first-session ad revenue (measure); manual lazy init can cause "used before init" crashes, so wrap behind interfaces.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• An SDK requires init in Application.onCreate by contract? → Ask the vendor; many only need it before first use, or call it on a background thread after super.onCreate with their documented thread-safety.
  • Gains on a flagship phone are tiny? → Optimize for p90 low-end cohort; flagships mask it.
  • Does multi-process matter? → A :push process pays Application init again; skip UI SDKs there via process name.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team halved cold start by deleting two providers and adding a Baseline Profile, then lost the gain in 3 months because nobody gated PRs on a startup benchmark.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "use threads", no measurement.
  • Hire: App Startup/lazy init, provider removal, Perfetto evidence.
  • Strong hire: Baseline Profile, receiver-triggered start, process-aware init, CI gates and ad-revenue trade-off.

questions.contextHtml: Release 12.0 of a ride-hailing app (3M DAU) was flagged by a pentest two weeks after rollout: another installed app can launch com.app.sdk.DebugOverlayActivity and a PushReceiver with crafted extras, reading the user's last-trip data in a log.
